questions.stem: In Earth and environmental science, a system is best defined as:
options: A set of interacting parts with a boundary, through which energy and matter may flow
A single living organism together with all of the food that it eats in a year
Any area of land that has been mapped and named by a government agency
A group of identical parts that do not affect one another in any way
questions.explanation: A system is made of components that interact, and it is defined by a boundary across which inputs and outputs of energy and matter can be tracked. The parts of a system influence each other, so a group of non-interacting parts is not a system.

questions.stem: Which statement describes an open system?
options: Both energy and matter can cross its boundary
Energy can cross its boundary but matter cannot
Neither energy nor matter can cross its boundary
Matter can cross its boundary but energy cannot
questions.explanation: An open system exchanges both energy and matter with its surroundings. A system that exchanges energy but not matter is a closed system, and one that exchanges neither is an isolated system.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a closed system?
options: Energy crosses its boundary, but matter does not
Matter and energy both cross its boundary freely
Neither matter nor energy crosses its boundary
Matter crosses its boundary, but energy does not
questions.explanation: In a closed system, energy such as light or heat can enter and leave, but the amount of matter inside stays the same. Open systems exchange both, while isolated systems exchange neither.

questions.stem: An isolated system is one in which:
options: Neither energy nor matter is exchanged with the surroundings
Only energy is exchanged with the surroundings, not matter
Only matter is exchanged with the surroundings, not energy
Energy and matter are exchanged, but only very slowly
questions.explanation: An isolated system exchanges neither energy nor matter with its surroundings. Truly isolated systems are an idealisation; a sealed, well-insulated flask is only an approximation because some heat always escapes.

questions.stem: Why is Earth as a whole usually treated as a closed system?
options: It receives matter from meteorites every day, but exchanges no energy with space
It exchanges neither energy nor matter with space because the atmosphere seals it
It loses large amounts of matter to space each year while gaining no energy at all
It receives solar energy and radiates heat to space, but exchanges almost no matter
questions.explanation: Earth gains energy as sunlight and loses it as infrared radiation, but the matter gained from meteorites or lost from the upper atmosphere is tiny compared with Earth's mass. That makes it approximately closed. It is not isolated, because energy flows in and out all the time.

questions.stem: A small creek runs through a patch of rainforest. Water, leaves and sediment flow in from upstream and out downstream, and sunlight falls on it. What type of system is the creek?
options: An isolated system
A static system
An open system
A closed system
questions.explanation: The creek exchanges matter (water, leaves, sediment) and energy (sunlight, heat) with its surroundings, so it is an open system. Most natural systems on Earth, such as rivers, forests and lakes, are open.

questions.stem: A student seals soil, water, a small plant and some snails inside a clear glass jar and leaves it on a sunny windowsill. Which type of system does the jar model?
options: An open system, because the plant and snails are still alive inside the jar
An isolated system, because the lid stops anything from entering or leaving
An open system, because water evaporates and condenses on the inside of the glass
A closed system, because light and heat cross the glass but matter stays inside
questions.explanation: Sunlight enters and heat leaves through the glass, but no matter crosses the sealed boundary, so the jar is a closed system. Evaporation and condensation inside the jar move water between parts of the system without any of it leaving.

questions.stem: A sealed vacuum flask of hot soup stays hot for hours. Why is it described as only approximately an isolated system?
options: Some heat still escapes slowly through the lid and walls
Matter enters the flask through tiny holes in the walls
The soup gains energy from the surrounding air over time
The soup is a liquid, and liquids cannot form a system
questions.explanation: A perfect isolated system exchanges no energy at all, but every real flask lets some heat escape, which is why the soup eventually cools. The sealed lid stops matter crossing, so the flask is close to isolated but not perfectly so.

questions.stem: Within Earth, matter such as carbon and water is recycled again and again, while energy is not. Which statement best explains the difference?
options: Matter enters as sunlight and leaves as heat, but energy mostly stays within the Earth system
Energy is destroyed by living things, but matter is created by them in photosynthesis
Matter is used up by plate movement, but energy is constantly made inside the core
Energy enters as sunlight and leaves as heat, but matter mostly stays within the Earth system
questions.explanation: Because Earth is close to a closed system, its matter cycles between the spheres, while energy flows through: it arrives mainly as sunlight and is eventually radiated back to space as infrared. Energy is transformed, not destroyed, and matter is not created by living things.

questions.stem: Which is an example of matter moving across the boundary of the Earth system, rather than within it?
options: A meteorite falling through the atmosphere and landing on the surface
Water evaporating from the ocean and falling as rain on a mountain
Carbon dioxide from a volcano being absorbed by a growing forest
Sediment eroded from a hillside being deposited on a river delta
questions.explanation: A meteorite brings matter from outside Earth across the boundary of the Earth system. Evaporation, absorption of carbon dioxide and sediment transport all move matter between spheres inside the system.

questions.stem: In a systems diagram of a coastal mangrove forest, which item is an output of energy?
options: Heat radiated from the leaves and mud
Sunlight falling on the mangrove canopy
Tidal water flowing in over the mud flats
Sediment settling among the mangrove roots
questions.explanation: Heat leaving the forest is an energy output. Sunlight is an energy input, while tidal water and settling sediment are flows of matter, the sediment being an input that is stored.

questions.stem: A dam is built on a river, so that far less sediment reaches the river mouth. Thinking of the coastline at the mouth as an open system, what is the most likely result?
options: Sediment input exceeds sediment output, so the coastline builds seaward
The coastline becomes a closed system, so its sediment stays unchanged
Energy inputs from waves stop, so the coastline no longer changes shape
Sediment output by waves exceeds sediment input, so the coastline erodes
questions.explanation: In an open system, a store grows or shrinks depending on the balance of inputs and outputs. If the river supplies less sediment but waves keep removing it, outputs exceed inputs and the shoreline erodes. Wave energy still arrives, so the system does not stop changing.

questions.stem: Which sphere of Earth includes the rocks, minerals and soils of the crust, together with the mantle and core?
options: Atmosphere
Geosphere
Hydrosphere
Biosphere
questions.explanation: The geosphere is the solid Earth: the crust, mantle and core, including rocks, minerals and soils. The hydrosphere is Earth's water, the biosphere its living things and the atmosphere its envelope of gases.

questions.stem: Groundwater stored in rock layers beneath the Great Artesian Basin is part of which sphere?
options: The hydrosphere
The atmosphere
The biosphere
The cryosphere only
questions.explanation: All of Earth's water, including oceans, rivers, lakes, ice and groundwater, is part of the hydrosphere. The water fills spaces in rock, but the water itself belongs to the hydrosphere rather than the geosphere.

questions.stem: The biosphere is best described as:
options: The upper part of the crust where soils form from rock
All of Earth's water in liquid, solid and gas form
All living things on Earth and the places where they live
The layer of gases surrounding Earth up to the stratosphere
questions.explanation: The biosphere includes every living organism and the parts of the other spheres they occupy, from deep-sea vents to the lower atmosphere. The layer of gases is the atmosphere and the water is the hydrosphere.

questions.stem: Which list contains only components of the atmosphere?
options: Nitrogen, granite, oxygen and sea ice
Oxygen, phytoplankton, ozone and argon
Water vapour, basalt, nitrogen and soil
Nitrogen, oxygen, argon and water vapour
questions.explanation: The atmosphere is the envelope of gases around Earth, mainly nitrogen and oxygen with argon, water vapour, carbon dioxide and other trace gases. Granite, basalt and soil belong to the geosphere, sea ice to the hydrosphere and phytoplankton to the biosphere.

questions.stem: Rain falls on a mountain, soaks into the soil and is taken up by tree roots. Which spheres does the water move between?
options: Biosphere to geosphere to atmosphere
Geosphere to biosphere to hydrosphere
Atmosphere to geosphere to biosphere
Hydrosphere to atmosphere to geosphere
questions.explanation: Rain falls from the atmosphere, enters the soil of the geosphere and is then absorbed by roots into the biosphere. The water itself is counted as hydrosphere throughout, but the question is which spheres it passes through.

questions.stem: Which process is an interaction between the geosphere and the atmosphere?
options: A fish taking in dissolved oxygen through its gills in a river
Seawater evaporating to leave a crust of salt on a tidal flat
A tree drawing water up from the soil through its roots
A volcano releasing sulfur dioxide and water vapour into the air
questions.explanation: A volcanic eruption transfers gases from the geosphere into the atmosphere. Gill respiration links the biosphere and hydrosphere, salt crusts link the hydrosphere and geosphere, and root uptake links the geosphere and biosphere.

questions.stem: Coral reefs build limestone from calcium and carbonate dissolved in seawater, using carbon that originally came from the air. Which sequence of spheres does this carbon pass through?
options: Geosphere, biosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere
Hydrosphere, atmosphere, geosphere, biosphere
Biosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere
Atmosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, geosphere
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide from the atmosphere dissolves in the ocean (hydrosphere), is taken up by corals (biosphere) and is locked into limestone rock (geosphere). This is one of the main ways carbon is stored for long periods.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a model of an Earth process, such as a diagram of subduction?
options: To reproduce every detail of the real process exactly at the same scale and speed
To prove the process is true so that it no longer needs to be studied by scientists
To replace field observations so that scientists no longer need to collect data
To represent a complex process in a simpler form that can be explained, tested or predicted
questions.explanation: Models simplify real processes so that they can be visualised, explained, tested and used to make predictions. No model reproduces every detail, and models are checked against observations rather than replacing them.

questions.stem: A textbook diagram shows an oceanic plate sinking beneath a continental plate at a smooth, straight angle, with a single red blob of magma rising to a volcano. Which feature of real subduction does this model leave out?
options: Subduction happens over millions of years along an irregular, curved and fractured slab
The oceanic plate is denser than the continental plate, so it is the one that sinks
Magma forms above the sinking plate and can rise to feed volcanoes at the surface
The continental plate sits above the oceanic plate where they meet
questions.explanation: A simple diagram shows a frozen moment, with a neat straight slab, while the real slab is curved, broken and moves over millions of years. The diagram does show that the denser oceanic plate sinks and that magma rises, so those are not omissions.

questions.stem: Students model subduction by pushing a sheet of paper (the oceanic plate) under a book (the continent) on a desk. Which is a limitation of this model?
options: The paper is thinner than the book, whereas real oceanic plates are thicker than continents
The paper is pushed by hand, whereas a real slab sinks mainly under its own weight
The paper goes beneath the book, whereas a real oceanic plate rides over a continent
The model shows two plates, whereas real subduction needs only a single plate
questions.explanation: Real slabs sink largely because cold, dense oceanic lithosphere is pulled down by gravity, not pushed from behind like the paper. The model correctly shows the oceanic plate going beneath the continent, and real oceanic lithosphere is generally thinner than continental lithosphere.

questions.stem: A computer model of a catchment predicts river flow after heavy rain. Its predictions match measured flows well for most storms but badly for storms after a long drought. What is the best response?
options: Stop measuring river flow, because the model already gives reliable predictions
Refine the model, for example by adding how dry soils absorb more water at first
Discard all of the model's predictions, because one mismatch proves it is useless
Trust the model over the measurements, because computers do not make errors
questions.explanation: When a model fails under particular conditions, scientists look for the process it leaves out and refine it. A model that works in most cases is still useful, and measurements remain the test of any model, not the other way around.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts a model of an Earth process with the actual process?
options: A model is simplified and usually changes scale or time, while the real process is more complex
A model is always larger than the real process, so it can show every grain of rock clearly
A model always works faster than the real process, so it is never useful for slow processes
A model includes every variable of the real process, so it never needs to be checked
questions.explanation: Models leave out detail and often compress time or scale, for example showing millions of years of plate movement in one diagram. Models can be smaller or larger and faster or slower than reality; what they share is simplification, which is why they must be checked.

questions.stem: A heated tank of oil with tea leaves is used to model mantle convection. The leaves rise above the heat source, spread across the top and sink at the far end within minutes. Which statement identifies a limitation of this model?
options: The mantle has no heat source, so convection cannot happen inside the real Earth
The tea leaves show the flow, so the model has no limitations for the mantle
The mantle is mostly solid rock that flows a few centimetres a year, not a runny liquid
Hot material in the mantle sinks and cool material rises, the opposite of the tank
questions.explanation: The mantle is solid rock that deforms and flows extremely slowly, so the real currents take millions of years, while the oil moves in minutes. The model correctly shows hot material rising and cool material sinking, and the mantle does have heat sources.

questions.stem: Two models of a volcano's eruption are compared. Model A is a physical model using baking soda and vinegar. Model B is a computer simulation using measured magma viscosity, gas content and vent shape. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Neither model has any value, because no model can include every factor that controls a real eruption
Model B can be tested against real eruption data and used for prediction, while Model A mainly illustrates the idea
Model A is more accurate because it uses real chemical reactions, while Model B only uses numbers on a screen
Both models are equally useful for predicting the next eruption, because both show material leaving a vent
questions.explanation: The baking soda model shows material being forced out of a vent but uses a different process from real magma and gas. A simulation built on measured properties can be compared with real eruptions and refined, which makes it more useful for prediction. All models are incomplete, but that does not make them worthless.

questions.stem: In science, a theory is:
options: A well-tested explanation supported by a large body of evidence
A guess that has not yet been tested by any observation
A single observation that has been repeated more than once
A fact that can never be changed by any new evidence
questions.explanation: A scientific theory, such as plate tectonics, is a broad explanation that has been repeatedly tested and is supported by many lines of evidence. It is not a guess, and theories can still be refined or replaced if new evidence demands it.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the difference between a scientific theory and a scientific model?
options: A theory is a physical object; a model is an idea that exists only in a scientist's mind
A theory is always mathematical; a model is always a diagram or a physical object
A theory is less certain than a model, because a model has been built and tested
A theory explains why something happens; a model represents it so it can be applied or tested
questions.explanation: A theory is a well-supported explanation, while a model is a representation (physical, conceptual, mathematical or computer-based) used to visualise, apply or test it. Models can be diagrams, equations or simulations, and neither type is limited to one form.

questions.stem: Continental drift was first proposed in the early twentieth century but was not widely accepted until evidence from the sea floor was gathered decades later. What does this show about scientific theories?
options: Theories gain acceptance as new evidence supports them and can be revised over time
Theories are accepted only when the scientist who proposed them is still alive
Theories are fixed once proposed, and later evidence is used only to illustrate them
Theories are accepted when most people vote for them, whatever the evidence
questions.explanation: Continental drift was developed into plate tectonics once sea-floor spreading and other evidence explained how continents move. Scientific ideas are accepted on the weight of evidence and are open to revision; popularity or the proposer's status does not decide them.

questions.stem: A model of Earth's interior shows a solid inner core, liquid outer core, mantle and crust. Why do scientists describe this as a model rather than a direct observation?
options: The interior was observed directly once, but the observations were later found to be wrong
No one has seen the interior, so the layers are inferred from evidence such as seismic waves
The layers change every year, so a photograph would be out of date by the time it was taken
Drilling has reached the core, but the samples were too hot to describe the layers accurately
questions.explanation: The deepest boreholes reach only about the upper part of the continental crust, so the deeper layers are inferred from indirect evidence such as seismic waves and meteorites. The layered structure is therefore a model built on evidence.

questions.stem: A new set of measurements disagrees with a well-established model of ocean circulation. Which response best reflects how science works?
options: Check the measurements, then test whether the model needs to be modified or extended
Reject the measurements, because established models are never contradicted by data
Abandon the model at once and replace it with the first alternative that is suggested
Ignore the conflict, because models and measurements are not meant to agree
questions.explanation: Scientists first check new data for errors, and if the data hold up, the model is modified or extended to account for them. A well-supported model is not dropped on a single result, but nor is it protected from evidence.

questions.stem: Which is a valid use of a scientific model of an Earth process?
options: Proving with certainty the exact date of the next large earthquake at a fault
Replacing all further measurement of the process once the model is published
Showing every single grain of sand moved by a river during a flood event
Predicting how sea level at a coast might change under different amounts of ice melt
questions.explanation: Models are used to make predictions under different scenarios, such as sea-level change. They cannot give certainty about events like earthquake timing, they never replace measurement, and they always leave out fine detail.

questions.stem: In a systems view of a freshwater lagoon on the Sunshine Coast, which is an input of matter?
options: Stormwater running in from the surrounding streets
Heat radiated from the water surface at night
Water evaporating from the lagoon in summer
Sunlight falling on the surface of the lagoon
questions.explanation: Stormwater brings water, sediment and nutrients into the lagoon, so it is a matter input. Evaporation is a matter output, radiated heat is an energy output and sunlight is an energy input.

questions.stem: A student draws a systems diagram for a eucalypt woodland near Toowoomba. Which pair correctly identifies one input and one output of the woodland?
options: Input: oxygen released; output: sunlight absorbed
Input: heat radiated; output: rainfall on the canopy
Input: rainfall; output: water lost by transpiration
Input: transpiration; output: carbon dioxide taken in
questions.explanation: Rainfall enters the woodland system and transpiration returns water vapour to the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide uptake and sunlight absorption are inputs, while oxygen release and radiated heat are outputs, so the other pairs are reversed.

questions.stem: Nutrient-rich runoff from farms increases nitrogen inputs to a coastal wetland, while outputs of nitrogen stay the same. Using a systems approach, what is the most likely result?
options: Nitrogen in the wetland falls, because inputs and outputs always balance
The wetland becomes a closed system, so no further nitrogen can enter
Nitrogen passes straight through, so stores in the wetland stay the same
Nitrogen accumulates in the wetland, which can lead to algal blooms
questions.explanation: When inputs exceed outputs, the store of that material within a system grows. Extra nitrogen fuels algal growth, which is a common water-quality problem in Queensland wetlands. Inputs and outputs do not automatically balance, and the wetland remains open.

questions.stem: Why is a local ecosystem, such as a patch of mangroves, classed as an open system rather than a closed one?
options: It exchanges energy with its surroundings, but no matter crosses its boundary
It exchanges nothing with its surroundings, because the roots trap all sediment
It exchanges matter with its surroundings, but no energy crosses its boundary
It exchanges both matter, such as water and nutrients, and energy with its surroundings
questions.explanation: Tides bring water, nutrients and sediment in and out, animals move across the boundary and sunlight and heat flow through, so the mangroves are an open system. A closed system would exchange energy but not matter.
